study.title: Romans 1 The promised gospel, the power to save and the universal guilt of mankind
study.overview: Romans 1 presents the opening of the letter with three main movements: Paul identifies himself as a separate servant and apostle for the gospel; then expresses his desire to visit the Christians of Rome and his willingness to proclaim the gospel there; finally, declares the central theme of the letter and begins the exposition of the sinful condition of the Gentile world. The chapter unites a promise fulfilled in Christ, salvation by faith, and the universal need for repentance before God's revelation in creation and human consciousness.

outline.title: Greeting and apostolic identity
outline.explanation: Paul presents himself as a servant of Christ Jesus, called to the apostolate and separated to the gospel of God. He connects the gospel to the promises made in the Scriptures, center it on the descending Son of David and confessed as the Son of God in power, and greets the believers of Rome as beloved and called saints.

outline.title: Thanksgiving, prayer and desire to visit
outline.explanation: Paul thanks God for the faith of the Romans, prays continually for them and wants to visit them to share some spiritual benefit and also receive mutual encouragement. He explains that he has tried to go, but was prevented, and reaffirms his debt to all peoples, being ready to preach also in Rome.

outline.title: The theme of the letter: the gospel and the righteousness of God
outline.explanation: Paul declares that he is not ashamed of the gospel, because he is the power of God for the salvation of everyone who believes, both Jewish and Greek. The gospel reveals the righteousness of God, received by faith, in harmony with the biblical affirmation that the righteous will live by faith.

outline.title: The wrath of God against Impiety and Human Degradation
outline.explanation: Paul shows that mankind suppresses the truth, although God has made his power and divinity evident in creation. In response to idolatry and refusal to recognize God, the Lord gives them over to their disorderly desires and a corrupted mind, culminating in a list of perverse practices and attitudes and in the approval of those who practice them.

study.context: The letter is addressed to the Christians who were in Rome, and the chapter itself indicates that Paul had not yet visited them. The text also shows that he wanted to reach them to strengthen the faith of the community and to proclaim the gospel where Christ had not yet been preached by him. The immediate context of the chapter is the presentation of the letter's thesis: salvation comes through the gospel, and the need for this salvation appears because all mankind is under the judgment of God.
study.theology: Romans 1 teaches that Jesus Christ is the center of God's promises and the content of the gospel. The identity of Jesus unites his true humanity, because he is a descendant of David according to the flesh, and his exaltation as the Son of God in power by the resurrection. The chapter also states that salvation is received by faith, not by human merit. At the same time, it reveals the reality of divine wrath against wickedness: the human being possesses some perception of God through creation, but this light is suffocated by idolatry, ingratitude and exchange of truth for lies. Divine surrender to sin shows both judgment and the gravity of human rejection of God. The final list of vices is not only a description of isolated behaviors, but a portrait of an entire disorderly society when it departs from the Creator.

scholarViews.insight: Paul may be echoing an ancient Christian creed or hymn in presenting Jesus as a descendant of David and declared the Son of God in power, to establish a common point with the Christians of Rome.
Paul calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ as a title of honor, not as relegation; his apostolic authority is born to have been called by Christ, not on his own initiative.

Knowing God's judgment means recognizing a moral rule that God himself has made known to a greater or lesser degree among nations; guilt increases when this truth is approved only in theory, but not obeyed.

questions: What changes in the way of reading the whole letter when we realize that Paul begins by uniting the Old Testament promise, lordship of Christ and salvation by faith?
In what practical ways today can a person "run the truth of God over the lie" even without using ancient religious images?
How can the church avoid both the shame of the gospel and moralistic hardship when talking about human sin?
study.practice: Read this chapter as an invitation to two concrete answers: first, trust in Christ as the center of God's promises and live by faith; second, examine his own life in the light of God's revelation, rejecting every form of idolatry, ingratitude and approval of sin. It is also worth practicing Paul's model: sincerely thanking for the faith of other Christians, praying for them and wishing for their spiritual strengthening before seeking any personal recognition.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not allow to accurately identify all the historical details of the church in Rome nor to confirm whether the initial greeting formally cites an ancient creed; this is an interpretive possibility, not a demonstrable fact only by this material. There is also no basis, in these notes, to expand beyond what the text says about the exact nature of the spiritual "gift" mentioned or about the historical extension of the philosophical references suggested by the commentators.
